blogs.title: The Future of SEO in an AI-Driven World
blogs.excerpt: How search engines are evolving with AI Overviews and answer engines — and what organizations need to do to stay visible.
blogs.content:
The future of SEO is being rewritten by AI. Google's AI Overviews, ChatGPT search and Perplexity now answer many questions directly — so ranking is no longer just about ten blue links. It's about becoming the source those AI systems trust and cite.

What is changing in search?

Search engines increasingly summarise answers instead of sending every visitor to a website. For high-intent queries such as "best dermatologist near me" or "piles treatment cost in Pune", users still click — but only on brands that appear credible, local and consistent across the web.

  • Answer Engine Optimisation (AEO): structuring content so AI can quote it accurately.
  • Entity SEO: helping search engines understand who your organization is, what it offers and where it operates.
  • Experience signals (E-E-A-T): real expertise, author credentials and reviews matter more than ever.

How to future-proof your SEO strategy

1. Answer real questions

Build pages and articles around the exact questions your audience asks. Use clear H2/H3 headings, short paragraphs and FAQ sections so both people and AI can scan them.

2. Strengthen your local entity

Keep your Google Business Profile complete, consistent NAP (name, address, phone) data everywhere, and a steady stream of genuine reviews.

3. Add structured data

Schema markup such as LocalBusiness, Person, FAQPage and BlogPosting tells search engines exactly what your content means.

4. Publish with authority

Show author names, qualifications and review dates on informational content. Link to trusted sources and keep older articles updated.

Key takeaway

SEO isn't dying — it's maturing. Brands that combine technical excellence, genuine expertise and helpful content will be the ones AI search recommends. Need help? Talk to the Codigix team about an AI-ready SEO audit.

blogs.title: Maintaining Accurate Local Business Profiles & Factual Listings
blogs.excerpt: Best practices for keeping hours, addresses, department details and service information accurate and consistent across digital directories.
blogs.content:
When people look for an organization online, they usually meet its directory listing before they meet its website. Outdated hours, a wrong phone number or a missing department creates confusion and erodes trust. Keeping listings accurate is routine maintenance, not marketing.

Details worth keeping correct

  • Legal or registered business name, written the same way everywhere.
  • Full address, map pin and contact numbers.
  • Opening hours, including holidays and temporary changes.
  • Departments or services offered, described factually.
  • Website address and accessibility information such as step-free entry.
  • Where it applies, factual fee information.

A simple maintenance routine

  1. Keep one source of truth. A single internal document that every listing is copied from.
  2. Name an owner. One person is responsible for updates and for reviewing public suggestions.
  3. Review on a schedule. Check every listing at least quarterly, and whenever anything changes.
  4. Remove what is outdated. Close duplicate listings and delete old services or locations.

Reviews and feedback

Do not write, buy or incentivise reviews, and do not filter who is invited to leave one. Reply to feedback politely and factually, and never include private personal details in a reply.

Regulated sectors

Healthcare institutions in particular should keep listings strictly factual. Avoid superlatives, ranking claims and promotional wording, and follow the communication rules that apply to the profession, such as the NMC, NDC or AYUSH guidelines.

blogs.title: Writing Clear, Responsible Public Health Information Online
blogs.excerpt: How to structure educational health content around clarity, source accuracy, appropriate practitioner disclosures and ethical communication standards.
blogs.content:
Good public health content informs people. It does not persuade them to choose a particular practitioner or promise a result. The points below help keep educational health writing clear, accurate and responsible.

Write for understanding

  • Use plain language and short sentences, and explain any technical term the first time it appears.
  • Lead with the main point, then add detail under clear headings.
  • Make pages accessible: descriptive headings, readable contrast and text alternatives for images.

Base every statement on a source

  • Rely on established guidance, such as national health authorities and peer-reviewed literature, and cite it.
  • Show the date a page was written and when it was last reviewed.
  • Where a case is discussed, use only properly de-identified, published journal material.

Attribute and disclose properly

  • When a medical professional writes or reviews content, show their name, qualification and registration details where required.
  • Label any content that was produced or edited with AI tools.
  • Do not use patient testimonials, before-and-after claims, star ratings, rankings or superlatives.

Avoid promotional framing

Do not promise cures or outcomes, use fear to prompt action, or offer inducements for care. The aim of the page is to help the reader understand a topic, not to bring in patients.

Respect privacy

Do not ask visitors to share medical records or health details through general contact forms. Collect only what is needed, explain why, and follow the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

This article is general information about communication practice. It is not medical or legal advice, and it does not replace the rules that apply to your profession.

blogs.title: Search Visibility & Structured Information in the AI Search Era
blogs.excerpt: How search engines process structured data and clear topical architecture, and practical steps organizations can take to keep information accurate and accessible.
blogs.content:
Search is changing. Search engines and AI answer features increasingly read how a page is structured, not just which words it contains. Organizations that present information clearly give these systems, and their readers, less to misinterpret.

What structured data does

Structured data is extra markup, usually schema.org vocabulary in JSON-LD, that describes a page in a machine-readable way: who the organization is, what services it offers, who wrote an article, or which questions a page answers. It helps search engines understand a page accurately. It does not guarantee any ranking or any special display in results.

Practical steps

  • One clear topic per page. Use a single descriptive heading and logical sub-headings so both people and software can follow the page.
  • Consistent organization details. Keep the name, address, phone number and opening hours identical across your website and every directory listing.
  • Add markup only for content that is visible. Organization, LocalBusiness, Article and FAQPage markup should describe what the page actually shows.
  • Clean technical foundations. Use readable URLs, an up-to-date sitemap, sensible internal links and fast, mobile-friendly pages.
  • Accessibility. Descriptive link text, alt text on images, good colour contrast and keyboard-friendly navigation help every visitor and support WCAG 2.1 AA alignment.
  • Visible dates and ownership. Show when a page was last reviewed and who is responsible for it.

Accuracy comes first

Markup must match the visible content. Do not mark up ratings or reviews you cannot substantiate, and do not make claims about search positions. Clear, truthful information serves readers better than any tactic aimed at search engines.

What to check regularly

  • Index and crawl status in Google Search Console.
  • Core Web Vitals and page-speed reports.
  • Structured data validation errors and warnings.
  • Accessibility checks on key pages and forms.

Search rankings depend on independent platform algorithms and cannot be guaranteed. This article is general information and not professional advice.
